what: New anti-racism standard will force Australian universities to use definitions of antisemitism and Islamophobia

Details of the anti-racism standard will be published on Monday as university bosses, students and academics prepare to appear at the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion. Higher education chiefs, academics and students to give evidence this week at royal commission Australian universities will be required to adopt definitions on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from next year, under a legally enforceable standard designed to stamp out discrimination on campuses. Details of the anti-racism standard will be published on Monday as university bosses, students and academics prepare to appear at the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion. A seperate set of governance principles will also become enforceable standards, including an obligation on public universities to publish vice-chancellor salaries, spending on consultants and the outcome of board meetings.

The introduction of a formal anti-racism standard was part of the antisemitism plan the federal government published after the Bondi massacre, and a recommendation from the Human Rights Commission’s landmark report on racism at Australia’s universities. The Respect at Uni report found racism was “systemic” on campuses, revealing cases of Palestinian students being mocked with shouts of “terrorism”, First Nations students being compared to “petrol sniffers” in lecture halls and Jewish students being fearful of attending class. Under the standard, the universities will be required to adopt a definition on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, create a “transparent” complaints process and issue guidances to students and staff. The universities are allowed to use their own definitions, including for antisemitism, meaning the institutions will not be forced to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition.

This rise in antisemitism sits within a broader rise in racist attacks in Australia.[7] These include, but are not limited to, rising Islamophobic violence,[8] anti-Arab[9] and anti-Palestinian[10] racist hate crimes, racist attacks against people of Indian heritage,[11] and racism towards First Nations people,[12] fueled by structural and systemic racism and inequalities. This trend mirrors patterns observed in other countries, including in the European Union[13] and the United Kingdom.[14] Antisemitism can also intersect with other forms of racism. For example, promoters of recent anti-immigration rallies in Australia have shared theories of the “Great Replacement" on social media.[15] The Great Replacement is an antisemitic conspiracy theory that “Jewish elites” are orchestrating the replacement of populations through non-white migration.[16]

Higher education chiefs, academics and students to give evidence this week at royal commission

Australian universities will be required to adopt definitions on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from next year, under a legally enforceable standard designed to stamp out discrimination on campuses.

Details of the anti-racism standard will be published on Monday as university bosses, students and academics prepare to appear at the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion.

A seperate set of governance principles will also become enforceable standards, including an obligation on public universities to publish vice-chancellor salaries, spending on consultants and the outcome of board meetings.

The introduction of a formal anti-racism standard was part of the antisemitism plan the federal government published after the Bondi massacre, and a recommendation from the Human Rights Commission’s landmark report on racism at Australia’s universities.

The Respect at Uni report found racism was “systemic” on campuses, revealing cases of Palestinian students being mocked with shouts of “terrorism”, First Nations students being compared to “petrol sniffers” in lecture halls and Jewish students being fearful of attending class.

Under the standard, the universities will be required to adopt a definition on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, create a “transparent” complaints process and issue guidances to students and staff.

The universities are allowed to use their own definitions, including for antisemitism, meaning the institutions will not be forced to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition.

payload.title: Australian yliopistoille tulee velvoittava rasisminvastainen standardi
payload.summary: Australian yliopistojen on ensi vuodesta lähtien määriteltävä antisemitismi, islamofobia sekä alkuperäiskansoihin kohdistuva rasismi. Oikeudellisesti velvoittava standardi edellyttää myös läpinäkyvää valitusmenettelyä ja toimintaohjeita.
payload.content:
Australian yliopistojen on ensi vuodesta lähtien otettava käyttöön antisemitismiä, islamofobiaa sekä aboriginaaleihin ja Torresinsalmen saarelaisiin kohdistuvaa rasismia koskevat määritelmät. Uusi oikeudellisesti velvoittava standardi on tarkoitettu ehkäisemään syrjintää kampuksilla ja ohjaamaan sitä, miten yliopistot käsittelevät rasismia koskevia ilmoituksia.

Standardin yksityiskohdat on määrä julkaista maanantaina. Yliopistojen johtajat, tutkijat ja opiskelijat valmistautuvat samalla antamaan tällä viikolla lausuntoja antisemitismiä ja yhteiskunnallista yhteenkuuluvuutta käsittelevälle kuninkaalliselle komissiolle.

## Yliopistot voivat laatia omat määritelmänsä

Yliopistojen on määritelmien lisäksi luotava läpinäkyvä menettely valitusten käsittelemiseksi sekä annettava opiskelijoille ja henkilökunnalle toimintaohjeita. Oppilaitokset saavat kuitenkin käyttää omia määritelmiään. Niitä ei siten velvoiteta hyväksymään esimerkiksi Kansainvälisen holokaustin muistoa vaalivan liiton eli IHRA:n antisemitismin määritelmää.

Virallisen standardin laatiminen sisältyi liittovaltion hallituksen Bondin verilöylyn jälkeen julkaisemaan antisemitismin vastaiseen suunnitelmaan. Samaa uudistusta suositteli Australian ihmisoikeuskomissio yliopistojen rasismia käsitelleessä Respect at Uni -raportissaan.

Raportissa rasismia kuvattiin järjestelmälliseksi ongelmaksi. Sen mukaan palestiinalaisopiskelijoita oli pilkattu terrorismiin viittaavilla huudoilla, alkuperäiskansoihin kuuluvia opiskelijoita oli halvennettu luentosaleissa ja juutalaisopiskelijat olivat pelänneet osallistua opetukseen.

## Rasistiset hyökkäykset ovat lisääntyneet

Human Rights Watchin mukaan antisemitismin lisääntyminen liittyy Australiassa laajempaan rasististen hyökkäysten kasvuun. Järjestö nostaa esiin islamofobisen väkivallan sekä arabeihin, palestiinalaisiin, intialaistaustaisiin ja alkuperäiskansoihin kohdistuneet viharikokset. Vastaavia kehityskulkuja on sen mukaan havaittu myös Euroopan unionissa ja Britanniassa.

Järjestö huomauttaa lisäksi, että antisemitismi voi limittyä muihin rasismin muotoihin. Esimerkiksi Australiassa järjestettyjen maahanmuuton vastaisten mielenosoitusten puolestapuhujat ovat jakaneet sosiaalisessa mediassa niin sanottua väestönvaihtosalaliittoteoriaa, jonka mukaan juutalaiset eliitit järjestäisivät väestöjen korvaamista ei-valkoisella maahanmuutolla.

Rasisminvastaisen standardin rinnalle tulee erillisiä velvoittavia hallintoperiaatteita. Julkisten yliopistojen on niiden perusteella julkaistava tiedot varakanslereiden palkoista, konsultteihin käytetyistä varoista sekä hallitustensa kokousten lopputuloksista.
summary_bullets: Australian yliopistojen on otettava rasisminvastaiset määritelmät käyttöön ensi vuodesta lähtien.
Yliopistot voivat laatia omat määritelmänsä, mutta niiden on järjestettävä läpinäkyvä valitusmenettely.
Uudistus perustuu havaintoihin järjestelmällisestä rasismista yliopistokampuksilla.

Higher education chiefs, academics and students to give evidence this week at royal commission Australian universities will be required to adopt definitions on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from next year, under a legally enforceable standard designed to stamp out discrimination on campuses. Details of the anti-racism standard will be published on Monday as university bosses, students and academics prepare to appear at the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion. A seperate set of governance principles will also become enforceable standards, including an obligation on public universities to publish vice-chancellor salaries, spending on consultants and the outcome of board meetings.

The introduction of a formal anti-racism standard was part of the antisemitism plan the federal government published after the Bondi massacre, and a recommendation from the Human Rights Commission’s landmark report on racism at Australia’s universities. The Respect at Uni report found racism was “systemic” on campuses, revealing cases of Palestinian students being mocked with shouts of “terrorism”, First Nations students being compared to “petrol sniffers” in lecture halls and Jewish students being fearful of attending class. Under the standard, the universities will be required to adopt a definition on antisemitism, Islamophobia and racism towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, create a “transparent” complaints process and issue guidances to students and staff. The universities are allowed to use their own definitions, including for antisemitism, meaning the institutions will not be forced to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition.

This rise in antisemitism sits within a broader rise in racist attacks in Australia.[7] These include, but are not limited to, rising Islamophobic violence,[8] anti-Arab[9] and anti-Palestinian[10] racist hate crimes, racist attacks against people of Indian heritage,[11] and racism towards First Nations people,[12] fueled by structural and systemic racism and inequalities. This trend mirrors patterns observed in other countries, including in the European Union[13] and the United Kingdom.[14] Antisemitism can also intersect with other forms of racism. For example, promoters of recent anti-immigration rallies in Australia have shared theories of the “Great Replacement" on social media.[15] The Great Replacement is an antisemitic conspiracy theory that “Jewish elites” are orchestrating the replacement of populations through non-white migration.[16]
